title: Dental Dos and Don'ts That Surprise People
author: Precision Dental
excerpt: Some dental advice is so familiar that nobody questions it, and a few widely held habits actively work against your teeth. These are the ones that come up most…
imageAlt: A woman in the dental chair with a clinician in gloves beside her
body:
Some dental advice is so familiar that nobody questions it, and a few widely held habits actively work against your teeth. These are the ones that come up most often in the chair.

Don't Rinse After Brushing

Most people brush, then rinse with water, then spit. That final rinse washes away the concentrated fluoride your toothpaste has just delivered, exactly when it would otherwise be strengthening the enamel.

Spit out the excess and leave it. If you use a mouthwash, use it at a different time of day rather than immediately after brushing, for the same reason.

Don't Brush Straight After Breakfast

Particularly after anything acidic: juice, citrus, coffee, or a soft drink. Acid temporarily softens enamel, and brushing in that window wears it away. Over the years this contributes to thinning, sensitivity and teeth looking more yellow as the dentine beneath shows through.

Either brush before breakfast, or wait around 30 minutes after. Rinsing with water in the meantime is fine.

Don't Stop Cleaning Where Your Gums Bleed

The instinct is to avoid an area that bleeds. The opposite is correct. Bleeding is usually a sign of inflammation caused by plaque, and the plaque needs removing for the gums to heal.

With consistent daily cleaning, bleeding usually settles within one to two weeks. If it does not, have your gums assessed, as gum and periodontal treatment may be needed.

Don't Brush Harder

Plaque is soft and comes away with light pressure. Scrubbing hard does not clean better; it wears enamel at the gum line and contributes to recession, exposing softer root surfaces that are more prone to decay and sensitivity.

Use a soft brush, and if you use an electric one, let it do the work rather than pressing it against the teeth.

Don't Use Charcoal or Bicarbonate Pastes Daily

Both work by abrasion. They lift surface stain and, over time, wear the enamel that keeps teeth looking light in the first place. The long-term result is often the opposite of what was intended.

If colour is your concern, professional teeth whitening addresses internal colour without abrading the surface.

Don't Use Your Teeth as Tools

Opening packaging, biting thread, holding hairpins and cracking nuts account for a surprising share of the fractures we see, often in teeth with large existing fillings that were already vulnerable.

A fractured cusp usually means a crown rather than a filling, and a crack that extends below the gum can mean losing the tooth entirely. It is a habit worth noticing and dropping.

Don't Assume Sugar-Free Means Safe

Many sugar-free drinks are just as acidic as their sugared versions. Acid erodes enamel directly, without any bacterial involvement, so a sugar-free soft drink sipped across an afternoon still causes damage, simply by a different route.

Sparkling water with added flavouring belongs in the same category, as do many sports drinks and kombucha.

Do Clean Between Your Teeth Daily

A brush reaches three of the five surfaces of each tooth. The two it misses are where a large share of decay and gum disease begins. Floss, interdental brushes or a water flosser, once a day, does more for your gums than anything else you can do at home.

Do Replace Your Toothbrush Often Enough

A brush or brush head is finished once the bristles splay, which is usually around three months of normal use and sooner for heavy-handed brushers. Splayed bristles do not reach along the gum line properly, which is exactly where plaque accumulates.

Replace it after illness as well, and store it upright and uncovered so it dries between uses.

Do Pay Attention to How Often, Not Just How Much

Each time something sweet or acidic enters your mouth, your teeth face an acid attack of 20 to 40 minutes. One dessert is one attack. The same amount grazed across an afternoon is several, with little recovery time between.

Reducing the number of eating occasions usually protects teeth more than changing what you eat.

Do Take a Chipped Tooth Seriously

A chip that does not hurt still deserves a look. Cracks can progress, and a small repair with a white filling now is a far better outcome than a crown or root canal treatment later. The same applies to a filling that has come out, even if the tooth feels fine.

Do Mention Jaw Ache and Morning Headaches

These are classic signs of grinding and clenching, which most people do not know they do. Grinding wears enamel permanently, and a custom night splint protects it. Nobody will spot this unless you mention it or we see the wear pattern.

Do Keep Attending When Nothing Hurts

Decay is painless until it reaches the inner layers of the tooth. Gum disease is painless until teeth loosen. Pain is a late signal, not an early one, which is the entire argument for a regular check-up and clean.

Ask Us Anything

If you have heard something about teeth and are not sure whether it holds up, ask at your next visit. Call Precision Dental on {{site:phone}} or book online.

faq.q: Should I rinse my mouth after brushing?
a: No. Spit out the excess toothpaste and avoid rinsing, so the fluoride keeps working on your teeth.

faq.q: Is it better to brush before or after breakfast?
a: Either works, but if breakfast includes anything acidic, brush before or wait around 30 minutes afterwards.

faq.q: Should I stop flossing if my gums bleed?
a: No. Bleeding usually means inflammation from plaque. Consistent daily cleaning usually settles it within one to two weeks.

faq.q: How often should I replace my toothbrush?
a: Around every three months, sooner if the bristles splay, and after an illness.

faq.q: Are sugar-free drinks safe for teeth?
a: They do not feed decay, but many are acidic and can erode enamel, especially when sipped over long periods.

faq.q: Do I need a check-up if nothing hurts?
a: Yes. Decay and gum disease are usually painless in their early stages, when they are simplest to treat.
